evaltense: We evaluated the prototype in two ways. First, we worked through every mission and lesson ourselves as learners
findings:
This was an informal review with one student, not a usability study across age groups.

What we found. The core loop of lesson, case and reflection was easy to follow, and the step bar at the top of every case made progress clear. We also noted five problems:

  • A first-time student lands on the map with no explanation of how a mission works, what badges and XP are for, or that the cases are fictional.
  • On the public site, a question a student types to a case character gets a scripted reply, and nothing says so. A new question can get a generic answer such as “Good question. What matters most to you here?”, which feels broken.
  • The Verify step shows the draft, sources, a browser and the verdict buttons at once, and its main instruction is in small gray text that is easy to miss.
  • Students’ chosen values do not appear during a case, only in the reflection afterward, so they have to remember them while making the decision the values are meant to guide.
  • The Fix it step in The Shortlist asks students to reach the “fair zone” without explaining the impact ratio or the 70% accuracy goal.
rec:
Be clear about what the AI case characters are. Label scripted replies as written by our team and live replies as Live, the same way Inside the machine labels Recorded run and Live. Before a typed question reaches the live model, run the same check Inside the machine uses for personal information and inappropriate words, and add a “Report this” button that switches the conversation back to scripted replies. We would also show the student’s top values during each case’s Decide step and add a short explanation of the fairness goal before Fix it.

Give teachers control.

cases:
In each case, the AI is a tool inside a fictional story, and students practice what we want them to do with real tools: question it, check it and decide what to do with its answer. We built the case AI in three layers, from most scripted to most open, so every case stays safe and solvable while still behaving like real AI.

Scripted AI tools with planted mistakes. Each case has an AI tool whose mistakes our team planted on purpose, as planned in our conceptual design. In The Confident Liar, students interview Nova, the newspaper’s AI writing tool. What a student types is matched by keywords to one of six topics (the mayor’s election, what she is known for, a quote, where to read more, Nova’s sources, or how sure Nova is), and Nova answers from our script. Every answer sounds confident, and asked “Are you sure?”, Nova says “Yes, I’m confident. This is well documented.” Three of its facts are wrong or cannot be confirmed: the year she became mayor, a quote she never said and a biography that does not exist. In the Verify step (Figure 5), students flag every checkable fact, then trace each one in a simulated browser of pages our team wrote, from a wiki anyone can edit back to the town clerk’s records, and rate it as confirmed, wrong or impossible to confirm. In Not Me, an online AI detector rates the fake video only 12% likely to be AI-made, while Nova, asked to compare the clip with the original, correctly shows which seconds were changed. Students see a tool that misleads and a tool that helps in the same case, which supports calibrated trust rather than blanket distrust.

Figure 7. The Confident Liar, Decide step. Students question the editor and the mayor’s granddaughter, using suggested questions or their own, before choosing what the newspaper should do.

Rule-based models students can test. Two cases let students change an AI’s inputs and watch its output change, which makes its logic visible.

  • RankRight (The Shortlist, Figure 8) is a scoring model we wrote as a set of rules. It scores applicants on ZIP code, school name, team sports, commute time, job experience and essay score. Students swap one detail of an application at a time, predict the new score and check it. In the Fix it step, they switch inputs on and off, and the model reports how many Eastside applicants make the top 60, its accuracy, and an impact ratio comparing Eastside’s selection rate with everyone else’s. The goal is a ratio of at least 0.8, the “four-fifths” rule used in U.S. hiring (Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, 1978), with accuracy of at least 70%. Turning off ZIP code while keeping commute time makes the model lean three times as hard on commute time, which shows how a stand-in can carry the same bias. Turning off real signals such as work history drops accuracy below 70%, which shows that removing data is not automatically fair.
  • Prompt Studio (The Confident Liar) checks the student’s rewritten prompt sentence by sentence for five ingredients: role, task, context, rules and format. It also checks whether the prompt includes the facts the student verified and tells Nova not to use the fake quote or book. Nova’s next draft is built from these checks, and each sentence is color-coded to the ingredient that shaped it, so students see what each part of a prompt changes.
  • Evidence ratings (Not Me, Figure 9). Students rate each of six leads as proving the video is fake, pointing to fake, proving nothing or pointing to real. A decision table checks each rating and explains it, and the verdict unlocks only after every lead is rated. Only the original video counts as proof.

Figure 8. The Shortlist. Students swap one detail of an application at a time to test RankRight, and can ask it to explain its scores.

Live conversations with characters. In each case’s Decide step (Figure 7), students talk to the people affected before choosing an option, such as the newspaper editor and the mayor’s granddaughter. They can tap suggested questions or type their own. When the prototype runs inside Claude, typed questions are answered live by Anthropic’s Claude model playing the character. Each request includes rules for every character: stay in character; answer in one to three short sentences; use only the facts our team wrote for that character, and say so in character rather than invent anything; never tell the student which choice to make; and keep it school-appropriate. It also includes the character’s role, its scripted answers as the only facts it may use, and the conversation so far. RankRight and Nova can be asked free questions the same way, with one extra rule: answer like the tool would, confidently, describing its own rules without revealing problems nobody asked about directly. We limited the characters to scripted facts because AI role-play tends to drift and invent details (Mollick et al., 2024). This keeps the planted mistakes where we put them and every case solvable. On the public GitHub Pages site, or if a live request fails, the same question gets a scripted reply instead.

Figure 9. Not Me, Investigate step. Students open each lead and rate how strongly it shows the video is fake.

Live replies are the only part of White Box that sends what a student types to an outside model, so they are also where our conceptual design’s safeguards matter most. The personal-information check used in Inside the machine does not yet run on case questions, and there is no “Report this” button. We return to this in our recommendations.
